    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/1806.07296v1</id>
    <title>End-to-End Neural Ranking for eCommerce Product Search: an application of task models and textual embeddings</title>
    <updated>2018-06-19T14:57:08Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.07296v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.07296v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We consider the problem of retrieving and ranking items in an eCommerce catalog, often called SKUs, in order of relevance to a user-issued query. The input data for the ranking are the texts of the queries and textual fields of the SKUs indexed in the catalog. We review the ways in which this problem both resembles and differs from the problems of IR in the context of web search. The differences between the product-search problem and the IR problem of web search necessitate a different approach in terms of both models and datasets. We first review the recent state-of-the-art models for web search IR, distinguishing between two distinct types of model which we call the distributed type and the local-interaction type. The different types of relevance models developed for IR have complementary advantages and disadvantages when applied to eCommerce product search. Further, we explain why the conventional methods for dataset construction employed in the IR literature fail to produce data which suffices for training or evaluation of models for eCommerce product search. We explain how our own approach, applying task modeling techniques to the click-through logs of an eCommerce site, enables the construction of a large-scale dataset for training and robust benchmarking of relevance models. Our experiments consist of applying several of the models from the IR literature to our own dataset. Empirically, we have established that, when applied to our dataset, certain models of local-interaction type reduce ranking errors by one-third compared to the baseline tf-idf. Applied to our dataset, the distributed models fail to outperform the baseline. As a basis for a deployed system, the distributed models have several advantages, computationally, over the local-interaction models. This motivates an ongoing program of work, which we outline at the conclusion of the paper.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37231v1</id>
    <title>TaskBridge: Technical Report for SIGIR 2026 eCommerce Challenge</title>
    <updated>2026-10-27T13:38:45Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37231v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.37231v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The SIGIR 2026 eCommerce Challenge Query Reformulation Task evaluates the reformulation of task-oriented queries into expressions suitable for product retrieval, followed by BM25-based retrieval. These queries often imply product needs through activity-level semantics, creating a lexical gap with catalog descriptions. Systems must preserve task intent while adapting the number of reformulations to the Automatic and Interactive protocols. We propose TaskBridge, a catalog-anchored framework comprising Catalog Semantic Anchoring, Unified Five-Candidate Rewriting, and Protocol-Aware Selection. It grounds queries in catalog vocabulary, generates five complementary reformulations, and selects one query for Automatic retrieval or up to four for Interactive retrieval using BM25 scores, query-product reranking, and weighted Jaccard overlap. The selected queries are independently executed using BM25 to produce results in the required six-column format. Experiments demonstrate improved retrieval effectiveness, with multiple complementary queries providing additional gains in the Interactive setting. TaskBridge achieved first place in the SIGIR 2026 eCommerce Challenge.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/1707.09258v1</id>
    <title>Patterns of Multistakeholder Recommendation</title>
    <updated>2017-07-28T14:42:34Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.09258v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1707.09258v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Recommender systems are personalized information systems. However, in many settings, the end-user of the recommendations is not the only party whose needs must be represented in recommendation generation. Incorporating this insight gives rise to the notion of multistakeholder recommendation, in which the interests of multiple parties are represented in recommendation algorithms and evaluation. In this paper, we identify patterns of stakeholder utility that characterize different multistakeholder recommendation applications, and provide a taxonomy of the different possible systems, only some of which have currently been implemented.</summary>
